previous.passage: Grapes have no business in Galway. Rory grows them anyway along the south wall of his workshop, and each October he presses them in a press he built before you, Aoife, became his apprentice. This year the press splits along one cheek. Rory has a glue for such repairs, made from a recipe he has never written down; for three years you have asked for it and been told you will learn it when you need it. He mixes it now while you watch, measuring nothing, talking about the weather. When you reach for a pencil, he sends you to the shed for clamps. Next morning he announces that his wrists are bad and the second batch is yours. You ruin it twice. On the third try he leans on the bench beside you, his wrists apparently healed, and tilts the pot a quarter-turn toward the window.
previous.question: Based on the text, why does Rory most likely claim that his wrists are bad?
options: He is embarrassed that age has made his hands unsteady for delicate work.
He hopes the failed batches will keep the recipe safely his own.
He is worn out from a long season of harvesting and pressing grapes.
He wants Aoife to learn the recipe through her own hands, not notes.
previous.explanation: 앞부분에서 Rory는 비법은 필요할 때 배우게 된다고 말하고, Aoife가 연필을 집자 창고 심부름을 보내 기록을 막는다. 이후 그는 손목이 아프다며 두 번째 배치를 맡기는데, 세 번째 시도에서는 손목이 멀쩡한 채 옆에서 냄비를 빛 쪽으로 돌려 색을 보게 해 준다. 두 단서를 함께 설명하는 동기는 직접 만들어 보며 손으로 익히게 하려는 것이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 손목이 곧 나은 점과, B는 그가 결국 도와준다는 점과 충돌하며, C는 수확 시기라는 배경만 보고 고른 오답이다.

previous.passage: I unfolded the scarf on the barge's narrow deck while the Red River slid brown and slow beneath us in Hanoi. It was mustard yellow, the one color I had refused to wear since childhood, and Faris, my younger brother's tutor, watched my face as though it were an exam he had studied for. My brother must have told him yellow was my favorite; my brother thought jokes were a form of love. I tied the scarf at my throat and said it matched the lanterns on the far bank. Faris let out a breath and began explaining, too quickly, how well the boy was doing with fractions. I nodded at every fraction. Along the bank, a woman was hanging fish to dry on a line of bamboo poles.

options: Faris is relieved, while Kainoa is indifferent to his nervous efforts.

previous.passage: Who decides what a nine-year-old is ready to hear? I put that question to Father Thiago on the Clyde bridge in the winter of 1987, though I had not set foot in his church for three years. My younger brother had asked me why our mother no longer came home, and I wanted the priest to give me an answer I could repeat. Thiago leaned on the cold stone and watched the river for a long while. Then he said that a hard truth told gently was a lantern, not a stone; the boy could carry it in front of him instead of on his back. I, Saoirse, the lapsed one, had expected scripture. Instead he offered me something I could use, and that night I sat on my brother's bed and told him plainly.

previous.passage: Wind hissed through the pines above the mountain bus stop near Porto Alegre, and my mother, Mingyu, smelled of the orange peel she always chewed when nervous. In our family, a rule had come down like an heirloom: a bride must not see the wedding road before the wedding day. I was the bride, Booker was the groom, and the only road to the chapel was this one. Every bus would carry me past it. My mother studied the timetable as if it were scripture, then folded it into a small square. Rules are coats, she said at last, cut for the shoulders of whoever first wore them. She tucked the timetable into my pocket, and when the bus came, she climbed on beside me without looking away from the road.

Solder smoke and old dust hang over the bench of a Gdansk radio repair shop. MARTA, seventy, bends over an opened receiver; KSENIA, nineteen, paces by the window.
KSENIA: Listen. Warsaw, Berlin, a station from Lisbon. Every one of them is somewhere I have never been.

previous.passage: Three things, brother Bartolo, I must set down before the festival: the shop owes four months' rent, the dock planks are rotting under our rehearsal spot, and you still play the second verse too fast.
